sentences.1: The farm foreman kept notes on his evening rounds.
sentences.2: He wrote that the shepherd had concluded the flock must be in the top field, since the gate stood open.
sentences.3: The foreman added, from what he saw himself, that the lower field was empty of grass.
sentences.4: The note ended with the time the rounds had finished.

readings_chosen: Sentence 1: "notes on his evening rounds" — readings: (a) notes kept during his evening rounds (temporal); (b) notes about his evening rounds (topical). Chosen: (b) topical; line note_topic is marked filled in and names the part I added, the link "about".
Sentence 1: "notes" and "the note" — readings: one running document, or several separate papers. Chosen: one document, named note throughout.
Sentence 1: "evening" — readings: part of the thing's name ("evening rounds"), or a when-qualifier. Chosen: when-qualifier, binned.

Sentence 2: "since the gate stood open" — readings: BECAUSE (the gate's being open produced the flock's location) or SINCE (the open gate is a reason to expect or believe it). Chosen: SINCE, because "must be" marks the step as an inference rather than a report of production.

Sentence 2: "the flock must be in the top field" — readings: asserting the flock's location outright, or holding it only as a conclusion. Chosen: the fact content is written and the modal "must" is binned; the hedge is carried by the TOLD standing in shepherd_world.

Sentence 2: "the shepherd had concluded" — readings: a reported act of concluding, or an attributed belief. Chosen: attributed belief; the attribution is binned and the content placed in the shepherd's own world, per the rule on who believes, wants or concludes what.

Sentence 3: "the lower field was empty of grass" — readings: a positive description of the field, or a denial of grass's presence. Chosen: positive Fact lower_field is empty of grass; no NOT is written, because the sentence does not phrase a denial.

Sentence 3: "from what he saw himself" — readings: a grounds mark (who knows what), or a SINCE link out of the foreman's act of seeing. Chosen: binned as an attribution of direct observation; a SINCE here would run out of an epistemic predicate the language has no form for.

Sentence 4: "the note ended with the time the rounds had finished" — readings: (a) the note's last item is a time entry, (b) the note's content simply runs out at that moment. Chosen: (a); the when is binned and the note's ending is tied to the rounds' finishing at line note_end.
